interactive.title: A measuring triangle on readings
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens. A graph has units on both axes: resistance R in ohms (Ω) up the side and temperature T in °C along, both starting at 0. Example readings of a motor winding sit as dots on a straight line that crosses the R axis well above the origin. A measuring triangle sits on the line; drag it along or stretch it by its corner. Its run is labelled in °C and its rise in Ω, and the readout divides the rise by the run, units and all, so the gradient shows in Ω per °C. It stays the same wherever the triangle sits and however big it is, because a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along. Where the line crosses the R axis a label reads 'R at 0 °C': T is 0 there, so the law's T part is 0 and only the intercept is left. The stretch of line below the first reading is dashed, because it is the line carried back past the readings, not a reading. Under the graph the law fills in, R = mT + c, with each number's unit beside it. Later screens show two windings' lines with a triangle on each, so you can see which sits higher and which climbs faster; a resistor's voltage against current, with a button that swaps the axes and flips the gradient's unit; a spring's force against its extension; and a lifting machine's effort against the load it lifts, where the intercept is the effort with no load on. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows a graph and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? fills in the working.
interactive.ignores: The readings are example values, made up for the lesson, and they sit exactly on a line; real readings scatter a little around one, which the next lesson deals with. The dashed part back to 0 °C is a prediction from the line, not a measurement, and it holds only as far as the real law stays straight. The lifting machine's intercept is read from its graph; this lesson does not say what causes it. Real windings, resistors, springs and machines have their own figures.

explain.text:
When readings from a test fall on a straight line, the line's rule is a [[law]] for what you measured, and its two numbers are real quantities with units. The gradient is how fast one quantity changes with the other, and the intercept is how much there is when the other is 0. In many materials, how strongly the material resists current changes with temperature in approximately a straight line.[^3] So take an example motor winding read at 20, 40, 60 and 80 °C, giving 10.8, 11.6, 12.4 and 13.2 Ω. These made-up readings sit exactly on a line, an ideal case; real readings scatter a little, and laying a line through them is the next lesson.

Put a step triangle on the line from 20 °C to 60 °C. Its run is 40 °C and its rise is 1.6 Ω, so the gradient is 1.6 Ω ÷ 40 °C = 0.04 Ω per °C.[^12] The rise is in ohms and the run in degrees, so dividing one by the other gives ohms per degree: a gradient's unit is y's unit per x's unit. Stretch the triangle to 80 °C and the run is 60 °C and the rise 2.4 Ω, still 0.04 Ω per °C, because a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along. So the winding gains 0.04 Ω for every degree it warms.

The intercept is the value of R where the line crosses the R axis,[^7] where T is 0. In R = 0.04T + c the 0.04T part is 0 there, which leaves c, so c is R at 0 °C, in ohms. Carry the line back 20 °C from the first reading: 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω. The law is R = 0.04T + 10. 0 °C lies below the readings, so the 10 Ω trusts the line to stay straight down there. Engineering syllabuses write the same law as y = ax + b, with a the gradient and b the intercept.[^5][^9] Each reading's ohms include that 10 Ω, so one reading divided by its temperature is not the gradient: 10.8 Ω ÷ 20 °C = 0.54 and 13.2 Ω ÷ 80 °C = 0.165, a different answer at each reading. That shortcut works only for a line through the origin, where c is 0. Use the law both ways: at 50 °C, R = 0.04 × 50 + 10 = 12.0 Ω, and a reading of 12.8 Ω means 12.8 − 10 = 0.04T, so T = 2.8 ÷ 0.04 = 70 °C.

Height and steepness are different things. A winding with R = 0.02T + 12 sits above one with R = 0.05T + 8 everywhere from 0 to 100 °C, yet the lower one gains 0.05 Ω for each degree, 2.5 times as fast. The same reading works on other laws. Plot a resistor's voltage up the side against its current along, and the gradient is its resistance,[^1] in volts per amp.[^2] Example readings of 6 V at 0.5 A and 24 V at 2 A give 18 V ÷ 1.5 A = 12 Ω. Swap the axes, current up the side, and the gradient flips to 1.5 A ÷ 18 V, about 0.083 A per V, which is not the resistance, so read the axis labels before you name a gradient. With force up the side and a spring's extension along, the gradient gives the spring constant,[^4] the force for each millimetre of stretch: 10 N at 4 mm and 30 N at 12 mm give 20 N ÷ 8 mm = 2.5 N per mm. **A straight-line law's gradient is how fast y changes with x, in y's unit per x's unit, and its intercept is the value of y when x is 0, in y's unit.[^9]**

analogy.text: For one billing period, an electricity bill against the units used is a straight-line law. The standing charge is the intercept, the pounds you pay with no units used, and the unit rate is the gradient, in pounds per kWh: pounds up the side and kWh along give a gradient in y's unit per x's unit, as ohms and degrees give Ω per °C.
analogy.breaks: A tariff is set before you use anything, so you know its two numbers in advance; with a winding you have only the readings and work the law out from them. And a tariff with a cheaper night rate is two lines, not one, while a winding's law is trusted only near the temperatures it was read over.

practice.text:
- Read the axis labels first: which quantity is up the side, and in what unit.
- Pick two points on the line far apart and draw the step triangle between them.
- Gradient = rise ÷ run, dividing the units too: y's unit per x's unit.
- Intercept: the value of y at x = 0. If 0 is off the graph or an axis starts above 0, work it out from a point as y − gradient × x.
- Write the law, then say each number in words with its unit.
- Check it with a reading you did not use.

**Rule of thumb:** the gradient is how fast, per one of x; the intercept is how much when x is 0.

**Worked example:** a winding reads 4.5 Ω at 25 °C and 5.5 Ω at 75 °C. Gradient = (5.5 − 4.5) Ω ÷ (75 − 25) °C = 1.0 ÷ 50 = 0.02 Ω per °C. R at 0 °C = 4.5 − 0.02 × 25 = 4.0 Ω. So R = 0.02T + 4.0: the winding would read 4.0 Ω at 0 °C and gains 0.02 Ω for each degree. Check at 75 °C: 0.02 × 75 + 4.0 = 5.5 Ω. At 40 °C it would read 0.02 × 40 + 4.0 = 4.8 Ω.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing one reading by its x. 5.5 Ω ÷ 75 °C is about 0.073, not 0.02, because the reading includes the 4.0 Ω at 0 °C.
- Taking the higher line as the steeper one. R = 0.02T + 12 sits above R = 0.05T + 8 from 0 to 100 °C but climbs less than half as fast.
- Turning the gradient upside down. 50 °C per Ω is the line read with the axes swapped, not its gradient in Ω per °C.
- Naming the gradient without reading the axes. With current up the side, a resistor's gradient is in amps per volt, and its resistance is 1 ÷ gradient.
- Using the first reading as the intercept. 4.5 Ω is R at 25 °C, not at 0 °C.
- Reading the intercept where a drawn axis starts. If the temperature axis starts at 20 °C, the line meets it at R at 20 °C, so work out R at 0 °C instead.
